Part 2 You will hear a guide talking to a group of
visitors to Pioneer Historical Village. First you have some time to look at questions 11
to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
Hello everyone and welcome to Pioneer Historical Village.
It's an outdoor park recreated to look just like a village from the mid 19th century.
Visitors can wander through the village, look inside the houses and get a feel for what life was like back then.
The village has grown somewhat since it was first opened to the public.
Going back a bit, in 1962 a committee was formed in the hope of preserving some of the local history.
Many years of planning and fundraising followed.
Volunteers worked throughout the 1970s to restore and move buildings to the site.
In 1980 the village welcomed its first paying visitors.
We'll go in now and I'll help you purchase your tickets.
Since there are 10 of you all together in this party, you qualify for the group discount.
The normal price of admission is $16 for adults and $12.50 for students and seniors.
But it'll only be $11 per person for all of you today, which is quite a saving.
Sometimes we have shows and demonstrations. We had hoped to show you how candles are made,
but the person organising it had to cancel at the last minute. You're all in for a treat of
another kind though. Just outside the shop we have an expert sweet maker who will be making lollipops
the old-fashioned way. So do go and have a look. If you want to make bread yourself,
head to the bakery and have a go. The space is quite small though so no spectators please.
You'll have a chance to interact with some farm animals today. We used to keep cows in the dairy
but someone had to be here twice a day to milk them and it became difficult to manage.
Chickens are everywhere though, not just on the farms. Every house kept a few for the eggs.
You're welcome to have a look and see if you can find any to collect.
Goats were another favourite animal, but they caused trouble too.
They're fun to feed, but they eat everything in sight.
The ones that we had have moved to a nearby farm.
Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15-20.
Now listen and answer questions 15-20.
Now, you'll probably want some time to explore the village. Please open your maps and we'll
have a look at the layout.
We'll enter through the main gate which is at the bottom of your map. So, if you'd like
to see the schoolhouse, that's a good first stop because it's not too far from the gate.
If you head directly north, you'll come to a beautiful old church. The schoolhouse
is diagonally across from it.
The mill is quite interesting, that's where they ground wheat to make flour for baking.
To find it, go straight up from the main gate until you get to the clock tower.
Turn right and it's on the other side of the road, across from the pond.
Then there are the stables where the horses were kept.
You may have seen the back of the stables already because they're a large building backing
on to the car park.
If you head west past the church, it's the first building you come to.
Medical care was quite basic in those days.
To get an idea of what it was like, you might like to visit the doctor's office.
Look in the middle of your maps, and it's in a block of three buildings that are all close together.
It's one of them.
There's even an old hotel.
Well, go up past the picnic area and the hotel is on the opposite side of the path near the pond.
Another place to see is the workshop.
It's at the end of that narrow winding path just south of the picnic area,
which is on the right hand side of your map at the eastern end of the village.
The village has been here since...
That is the end of part two.
You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to Part 2.
You will hear two environmental study students called Annie and Ryan discussing with their
tutor a presentation they will give on disposing of dangerous household waste products.
Do you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24?
Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
Hi Annie, Ryan, come in.
Morning.
I know you want to discuss your project presentation.
Start by reminding me what you're focusing on.
We've been looking at a research article on the disposal of hazardous household waste.
That includes things like dangerous chemicals we use in the home,
but also less obvious items like electrical equipment, which are potentially really polluting
as well. The research basically involved interviews, trying to find out what influence
the methods people use to get rid of their dangerous waste. There were some really surprising
results about people's behaviour and attitudes with regard to waste disposal.
Yeah.
It's no great shock that in general people are much more aware than they used to be.
you know, about the effects of these materials on the environment and about the value of
careful disposal, even the smallest, cheapest things.
Yes, but I did think it was surprising that people don't get very enthusiastic about the
subject of waste disposal, like they do about other aspects of environmental protection.
Me too.
Apparently, they find it all rather tiresome.
Another striking thing was that many people are more careful when they're
using certain hazardous materials than when they are getting rid of them.
At that stage, they simply don't remember that they'll be bad for the environment.
Absolutely. That really amazed us.
I can see why. But were there any positives? Hope for the future?
Well, in the conclusion section of the article, they talked about ways to improve recycling
rates in the local area.
And I think some of the ideas would improve things around here, you know?
The article talked about laws in certain countries that certain types of waste have
to be disposed of safely or you are taken to court.
I think financial penalties are a good idea, but criminalising people is too harsh.
I think it's more effective to impose a penalty on homes if they don't recycle stuff.
I still think legislation forcing local councils to increase recycling rates works better.
You can present both ideas.
Yeah, and agree to differ.
I think encouragement is always better in the long run and getting the local community involved
such as schools, working with kids. That way you establish good habits which last throughout
their lives. Okay.
Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25
to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
Do you want to talk through your actual presentation?
Yes, we thought we'd talk about different types of waste covered in the research and give advice on each one.
That's a great idea.
We thought we'd start with paint.
Yeah, we'll explain that we advise setting up schemes where you can take it to a centre to be used by people who need it.
repainting an elderly person's home, for example, like they do in many parts of the world.
Yes. Which is a positive note to start on.
And will you discuss batteries?
Definitely. They're so small that they're the simplest things to drop in a bin and forget.
And I think we should emphasise that people should have a storage container at home
where they can put them until they've got enough to take to a central collection facility
because they're full of toxic substances.
Medicines are really interesting.
I imagine people don't think of them as dangerous.
No, indeed.
The point we want to make is that, as a rule, things like antibiotics
should not need to be thrown away in the first place
Because doctors usually tell us we should finish off the whole course of tablets.
So there aren't any left to go for waste.
Doubly good strategy.
Are you discussing pesticides?
Yes. The point we highlight from the article is that people are often unsure what to do with them.
And there needs to be clearer information given on the packaging so people are left in no doubt.
We thought we'd also look at tyres. Rather than sending them to the dump, people should be encouraged to be creative with them.
Not just sending them away to be re-cut for re-treads, but to make them into things like plant holders for your garden.
Good, yeah. And will you mention any electrical appliances?
We've opted to finish with fridges, because this is actually a good news story.
The fact that we now have the capacity to use less dangerous materials.
And we should continue to exploit that capacity to reduce effects on the ozone layer.
Good. Well, that seems...
That is the end of Part 3. You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to Part 3.
Part 4 You will hear part of a student presentation
about a field trip to a whale shark research center given to fellow marine biology students.
You have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
Hi everyone.
I've just returned from my field trip
and want to share some of my experiences with you.
I learned a lot about whale sharks on this trip.
For example, they're actually the largest species of fish
in the world seas, about the size of a bus.
Despite their massive size,
whale sharks are docile animals.
Because of the name, you might be confused
about whether these animals are whales or sharks.
They are in fact sharks,
but they do have some things in common with whales.
They're similar in terms of their large size
and what they eat.
Like many species of whales,
their diet consists mainly of plankton and krill,
which are tiny plants and animals.
Unlike many whale species,
they prefer to swim close to the surface of the water
rather than cruising the depths of the ocean.
So that's a key difference relating to their habits.
Another one relates to their physical makeup.
Their skeleton is made entirely of cartilage
in comparison to whales
that have skeletons made of real bones.
The place I visited is called Ningaloo in Western Australia.
We were there to observe a large group of whale sharks
which congregate in that part of the ocean
each year between April and July.
Ninkaloo is ideal for whale sharks
because there is a coral reef nearby
which ensures an abundant supply of food.
It's great for divers too
because although it's in relatively deep waters,
the reef is in close proximity to the shore.
Unlike some reefs that you have to travel miles to get to.
I'd like to move on now to tell you
about the Whale Shark Research Centre
and the research being conducted there. We know that whale sharks are migratory,
but not a lot is known about where they go and why. The methods currently being
used to monitor them could be better. One way is to use an electronic tracking
device or TAG, which researchers have to attach manually to the fin. It's not an
easy process and the tags are also quite expensive so if it falls off you're
trouble. Another way of monitoring whale sharks is with a special drone to spot
the animals in the ocean. This can give you a rough idea of numbers but obviously
it's not an exact science. The researchers at Ningaloo are involved in a
new research project that's currently being carried out to investigate whale
shark feeding habits. They hope to find out more about how far whale sharks
travel to feed. They're using an innovative approach to do this which
analyzes plankton. Apparently plankton from different places contains different
quantities of carbon types. The researchers are checking the plankton
consumed by the whale shark against maps which have all the different plankton
zones marked on them. This comparison allows them to track exactly where the
whale shark has been feeding. Some research that I was involved in on my
field trip was directly observing the whale shark behaviour. This was part of a small study being
carried out in Ningaloo to find out how whale sharks are affected by human activity. We drifted
along in our boat with the engine off, then when a whale shark was nearby we switched on the engine.
We noticed that the resulting noise affected the behaviour of the animal. As soon as it
and was quite obvious. One day we got to witness the great work they're doing at
the centre to educate the community about whale sharks. At the moment there's a
whale shark race. The researchers select a mature whale shark which has been
tagged and they allocate it to a school. The children get to track the journey
of their whale shark and see which one travels the furthest. All the data
is on the website. It's clear that these majestic creatures require careful
conservation and management. With humans and whale sharks being in close
proximity, problems can occur. While these events may be rare, all injuries
which whale sharks suffer must be documented with information such as
date and location and a photograph if possible. The Fisheries Department has
agreed to keep these records in their digital image library.
Something that is being introduced next year in Ningaloo is a code of conduct. It covers
the rules that need to be followed to minimise any distress to the sharks. Scuba diving is
not going to be allowed anymore, as previous research has found that whale sharks find bubbles
disturbing.
Another new rule is that boats will...
That is the end of part 4. You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
